title: Canada's Oil Pivot to Asia Hits Full Capacity as Uganda Prepares First Exports; Uzbekistan Cuts Rosatom Ties
subhead: With Hormuz flows still constrained, non-Gulf supply routes are moving to the fore: Canada's Trans Mountain is running at full capacity with expansion planned, Uganda is set to become an oil exporter in early 2027, and Uzbekistan is scaling back its nuclear cooperation with Russia. Brent trades near $99 as fresh attacks on Saudi energy sites keep the Gulf risk premium elevated.

sections.heading: Canada's Oil Pivot to Asia Reaches Full Capacity
sections.body:
Canada's long-promised shift toward Asian buyers is now materializing in the numbers. The Trans Mountain pipeline is running at full capacity, and producers are planning an expansion, according to OilPrice.com. The 890,000 bpd line to the Pacific coast — which took years and billions in cost overruns to complete — is now the main artery for Canadian crude reaching Asian markets, a route that has gained strategic weight as Gulf flows through Hormuz remain constrained.

Western Canadian Select (WCS) is trading at $79.13, with premium synthetic grades near $91.88, reflecting firm demand for non-Gulf barrels. The expansion talk signals that Canadian producers see Asia as a durable outlet, not a temporary workaround.
sections.whyItMatters: Every barrel that bypasses Hormuz reduces the Gulf's pricing power. Canada's full-capacity Trans Mountain and planned expansion give Asian refiners a growing, war-free supply alternative — a quiet but real shift in the geography of global crude trade.

sections.heading: Brent Nears $99 as Saudi Energy Sites Hit Again
sections.body:
Oil prices pushed toward the $100 mark on Tuesday, with Brent at $98.70 and WTI at $94.12 (+2.89%) in Asian trade, after fresh attacks on Saudi energy sites, OilPrice.com reported. The Jizan refinery (400,000 bpd) was hit again Monday, and the southern region bordering Yemen saw fires, injuries and temporary shutdowns. Jizan recorded no exports in August, per the Financial Times, as Houthi attacks have repeatedly knocked the facility offline.

Live prices Wednesday morning show Brent at $99.31 and WTI at $94.29, with the OPEC basket jumping 8.76% to $106.30 and Murban at $110.80 (+3.75%). Anadolu Agency put Brent at $98.47 on Tuesday, citing US-Iran tensions and fears of disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: The repeated strikes on Jizan show the Houthi campaign is now a sustained supply-side threat to Saudi refining and export capacity, not a one-off. With Brent knocking on $100, the market is pricing in a prolonged Gulf risk premium.

sections.heading: Gulf Producers Restore Exports via Ship-to-Ship Workarounds
sections.body:
Gulf producers are adapting to the Hormuz disruption. Kuwait's exports have rebounded to roughly 1 million bpd — about two-thirds of the pre-war 1.6 million — using ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait, OilPrice.com reported. Qatar and Kuwait have restored about 70% of pre-war export volumes by shuttling cargoes and transferring them at sea. Total Hormuz flows are estimated at around 10 million bpd (9 million crude plus 1 million fuels), down from roughly 20 million before the war.

Buyers now pay a premium for delivery outside the strait, while cargoes loaded inside the Gulf carry discounts. The workarounds are costly and add days to voyages, but they are keeping Gulf crude moving.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is learning to live with a partially closed Hormuz through STS transfers and rerouting. But the added cost and complexity are baked into prices, and ANZ's Daniel Hynes sees no full return to pre-war throughput until late Q1 or early Q2 2027.

sections.heading: Refining Squeeze Deepens as Fuel Markets Tighten
sections.body:
The crude story is only half the picture. Vitol CEO Russell Hardy described global fuel markets as 'pretty, pretty tight and inflexible,' with refined product inventories still drawing and not enough refining capacity to meet demand, OilPrice.com reported. US refinery utilization is at 98%, with Midwest peaks above 103% — a level that is not sustainable. Middle distillate cracks are at record highs, and Russia has banned diesel exports until at least the end of September.

ING notes the 'global refining system has little slack.' Goldman Sachs' Daan Struyven warns oil could hit $120 if shipping attacks intensify, adding that supply shocks are 'bigger than in the crude market' for gas and fuels.
sections.whyItMatters: The bottleneck is no longer just crude supply but the refining system itself. With utilization maxed out and Russia withholding diesel, product prices — gasoline, diesel, jet fuel — are where the war's cost is hitting consumers hardest.

sections.heading: Russia Vows to Keep Supplying India Despite US Tariff Threat
sections.body:
Russia's Ambassador to India, Denis Alipov, said Russia will remain a key crude supplier to India and is 'ready to supply as much oil as India needs,' warning that 'the world will not cope if Russian oil is excluded,' OilPrice.com reported. The comments come as the US 'bill from hell' — Senator Lindsey Graham's proposal for 100% tariffs on the biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas — has passed the Senate 86-11 but remains deadlocked in the House.

India's Russian oil imports eased in August from July's record high, but Moscow is signaling it will defend its position in the Indian market regardless of US pressure.
sections.whyItMatters: The Graham tariff bill is the sharpest US attempt yet to weaponize trade against Russian energy buyers. India's response — and whether it bends to US pressure or deepens Russian ties — will shape the global crude market's center of gravity.

sections.heading: China's Crude Imports Rebound as Fuel Exports Jump 29%
sections.body:
China's crude imports recovered to 8.93 million bpd in August, up 6.2% from July, bouncing back from the decade-low 7.1 million bpd seen in June, OilPrice.com reported, citing Tsvetana Paraskova. Imports remain 23.4% lower than a year ago, but the direction is up. China's fuel exports jumped 29% to 6 million tons in August, and Beijing boosted buying of Russian ESPO grade crude while also turning to Argentina.

China amassed roughly 1.4 billion barrels of strategic reserves before the war, giving it a buffer that lets it buy opportunistically rather than at any price.
sections.whyItMatters: China's rebound — and its preference for discounted Russian ESPO — shows Beijing is using its reserve buffer to buy selectively while Moscow locks in its largest customer. The US tariff threat against Russian oil buyers directly targets this relationship.

sections.heading: Uzbekistan Scales Back Nuclear Cooperation With Russia
sections.body:
Uzbekistan is pulling back from its nuclear partnership with Russia. Tashkent is seeking more control over the $9.5 billion Rosatom project and has formed a new consortium with international engineering firms, OilPrice.com reported. Notably, Rosatom was not mentioned in the September 2 announcement about the project's next phase.

The move signals Central Asia's cautious recalibration of energy ties with Moscow, even as Russia remains the region's dominant nuclear supplier.
sections.whyItMatters: Uzbekistan's step back from Rosatom is a small but telling sign that Russia's nuclear export leverage is fraying at the edges, as Central Asian states diversify their energy partnerships amid the broader geopolitical realignment.

sections.heading: Uganda Set to Become World's Newest Oil Exporter in Early 2027
sections.body:
Landlocked Uganda is moving toward first oil. The Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC) has appointed Vitol to market its Pearl Sweet crude, with exports expected in early 2027, OilPrice.com reported. The crude, produced by TotalEnergies and CNOOC at the Tilenga and Kingfisher fields, has a low sulfur content of 0.12% and will flow through the $5 billion East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), now more than 90% complete, to Tanzania's port of Tanga.

Uganda's Energy Minister Monica Musenero Masanza presented Pearl Sweet to refiners and traders at the APPEC 2026 conference on Tuesday.
sections.whyItMatters: Uganda's entry adds a new, non-Gulf, non-Russian supply source to the global market at a moment of maximum supply anxiety. The EACOP's completion — after years of delays and controversy — is a concrete win for African energy sovereignty.

bottomLine: The Gulf war keeps Brent near $99 and keeps the refining system stretched, but the day's most consequential moves are happening outside the conflict zone: Canada's Trans Mountain is at full capacity with expansion planned, Uganda is set to become an oil exporter in early 2027, and Uzbekistan is stepping back from Rosatom. Russia is digging in to defend its Indian market against the US tariff bill, while China's crude imports rebound on discounted Russian barrels. The market is not just pricing a war — it is quietly redrawing the map of who supplies the world's oil.
sources: OilPrice.com (Canada Asia pivot, Brent near $99, Gulf workarounds, Vitol CEO, Russia-India, China crude, Uzbekistan nuclear, Uganda exporter), Anadolu Agency, Financial Times (via OilPrice.com), ING, Goldman Sachs, ANZ
